t: the musaf of the day. Offerings brought on Shabbatot and festivals in addition to the daily tamid offering (for the musafim of Yom Kippur see also Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 10:1).

and a sin-offering goat is done outside. Its blood is thrown on the outer altar and its flesh is eaten by the kohanim (like a regular sin offering), unlike the goat mentioned next, which comes as part of the special obligations of the day and whose blood is thrown inside, in the Sanctuary, and whose flesh is burned.
and it is eaten at night. After Yom Kippur ends, since it is forbidden to eat on Yom Kippur.
and further they offer in addition to this musaf. Besides the musaf offerings, on Yom Kippur they offer additional offerings that have special laws.
a young bull as a sin offering, and it is burned. Its flesh is burned, unlike a regular sin offering whose flesh is eaten by the kohanim.

and a ram as a burnt offering. Its law is like other burnt offerings, except that it is purchased with the High Priest's money and not with public funds, and therefore it is not included in the musafim of the day (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:6).

and the ram from the community mentioned in the portion Acharei Mot, etc.. The people's ram mentioned in the description of the Yom Kippur service in the portion Acharei Mot (Leviticus 16:5) is the same ram that is mentioned in the list of musafim in the Book of Numbers (29:8), and these are not two separate offerings.
and the second, the scapegoat. The goat for Azazel that is sent to the wilderness (see below chapter 3).
fifteen. Not counting the scapegoat, which is not considered an offering.

whether the one anointed with the anointing oil or the one invested with the garments. The High Priest is appointed by being anointed with the anointing oil and wearing the High Priest's garments, and he is called "anointed with the anointing oil." When no anointing oil is available, his appointment is by wearing the garments alone, and he is called "invested with the garments" (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:12-13, and see ibid. 1:8). Both are fit for the Yom Kippur service.
with a married High Priest. And he must be married to only one wife (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 5:10).

to his chamber in the Temple. A special room of the High Priest that was in the Temple courtyard (this chamber was also called "the wood chamber" and "the Palhedrin chamber" - Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:17; and see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 5:7).
a tradition from Moses our teacher. It was handed down by tradition to the sages of Israel from Moses our teacher (and similarly see Hilchot Parah 2:2).
lest she be found a niddah. At the time of relations with her.
and he is found impure for seven days. As is the law of one who has relations with a niddah (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 3:2).
and he cannot serve. For it is forbidden to serve while impure.
and they prepare another High Priest for him. They designate one of the kohanim to be ready to replace the High Priest in case he is unable to serve.

whether a disqualification befell him... the one who enters in his place does not need investiture, rather his service invests him. Generally the appointment of a High Priest is by anointing him with the anointing oil and dressing him in the eight garments of the High Priest, the golden garments (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:12-13). If on Yom Kippur a High Priest must be appointed in place of this one who was disqualified, even if it happens after the offerings were brought, when the service is done in white garments, his investiture is accomplished by the very service of Yom Kippur, which is permitted only to a High Priest.

and all the commandments of the High Priesthood are upon him. Even after the High Priest was restored and this kohen left his post, all the special prohibitions of a High Priest apply to him as well (such as the prohibition of marrying a widow and others).

except that he does not serve as a High Priest. He does not serve in the Temple in the eight garments because of enmity. And he also does not serve in four garments, since his status is that of a High Priest.
and if he served. In the eight garments.

they sprinkle on him from the ashes of the red heifer on the third day from his separation and on the seventh. The purification of one impure with corpse impurity is by sprinkling on him from the ashes of the red heifer on the third and seventh days of his impurity, and if he waited several days after his impurity, when he comes to be purified he counts three days and then they sprinkle on him (see Hilchot Parah 11:1-2).
and if Shabbat falls. For it is forbidden to sprinkle on it (see Hilchot Shabbat 23:8).
they postpone the sprinkling. And they do not sprinkle on the High Priest at all that year.
throws the blood. Of the tamid offerings.
and burns the limbs of the tamid. He burns them on the outer altar.
elders from the elders of the court. Judges from the Great Sanhedrin (Aruch HaShulchan 158:15).
and they read before him. The order of the Yom Kippur service from Scripture in the portion Acharei Mot (Leviticus chapter 16).
the Yom Kippur service and its order. All the laws of the offerings, the confessions, and the incense service explained below.
my master. My lord (a term of respect toward the High Priest).

or perhaps you have not learned this matter. In the Second Temple period the High Priests were appointed by the kings according to their wishes, and then it was possible that the High Priest had never learned the laws of the service (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 1:3).
at the eastern gates. At the eastern gate of the Temple courtyard.
so that he will be familiar and accustomed to the service. So that he will be skilled in the service and in identifying the animals on Yom Kippur.
at dusk. Toward darkness, at midday.
they did not let him eat much. Of all kinds of foods.
and they did not let him sleep. They did not let him sleep all night on the eve of Yom Kippur.
lest he see an emission. In his sleep.
and they did not feed him. At all, not even a little.
things that cause emission of semen. That increase semen.
heresy sprouted in Israel and Sadducees emerged. The sect of the Sadducees arose, who did not believe in the Oral Torah.

and they used to say that the incense of Yom Kippur, etc.. On Yom Kippur the High Priest burns incense inside the Holy of Holies (below 4:1). According to the Sadducees, the incense must be placed on the coals outside the Holy of Holies, so that his entry into the Holy of Holies would be within the cloud of incense.
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.

we adjure you, etc.. Because it is forbidden to be in the Sanctuary when the High Priest enters the Holy of Holies (see Leviticus 16:17) and there is no way to know what the High Priest does, they would adjure him (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 1:5). And they adjured him in the chamber called Beit Avtinas.
by Him who caused His name to dwell in this House. By the Holy One, blessed be He.
that you will not change anything of all we told you. And that you will burn the incense according to the tradition of the Sages.
concealed. Unknown.
perhaps he has nothing in his heart. And it is forbidden to suspect one whose actions are concealed except out of necessity (ibid.).
in the Holy Writings. The books of Ketuvim (such as Job, Ezra, and Chronicles - Mishnah Yoma 6:1).
young Levites. Young Levites.
they snap before him with the tzereda finger. Striking the finger (next to the thumb) against the thumb, to make a sound (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 1:7).
stand and cool yourself. The kohanim were barefoot during their service in the Temple, and standing on the floor could cool and rouse the High Priest.
until the time of slaughtering arrives. Before sunrise, when the whole east lights up (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 1:1).
dressed in golden garments. In the eight garments in which the High Priest serves all year round (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 8:2).
in white garments. Four linen garments: tunic, trousers, sash, and turban (see ibid. 8:3).
the bull offering... and the two goats, etc.. Below 3:4-7.
and the burning of the incense in the Holy of Holies. Below 4:1-2.

whenever he changes the garments and takes off the garments and puts on other garments, etc.. Every change of garments from golden garments to white or the reverse requires immersion (but changing from ordinary clothes to priestly garments does not require immersion by Torah law, as below halakhah 3).

and he shall take off the linen garments, etc.. The verse speaks of immersion between taking off the white garments ("linen garments") and putting on the golden garments ("his garments"), and the same law applies in reverse.
immersion. Immersion of his entire body in a mikveh.
sanctification. Washing the hands and feet.
the ordinary garments on him. His private clothes that do not belong to the Temple service.
and dries himself. Wipes himself dry.
and slaughters the tamid... and burns the limbs of the tamid with the chavitin and the libations. As is done in the Temple every day (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin chapter 6).
the chavitin. A meal offering that the High Priest would offer every day as part of the order of service in the Temple.
and performs the entire service of the day. The services specific to Yom Kippur.
the confessions. Over the bull and over the scapegoat sent to Azazel (below halakhah 6).
the lottery. In which they cast lots to determine which of the two goats will be offered to God and which will be sent to Azazel (below 3:1).
and the throwing of the blood inside. Throwing the blood of the bull and the goat in the Holy of Holies and in the Sanctuary (below 3:5).
and hands over the goat to the one who sends it to Azazel. Below 3:7.

and removes the sacrificial parts of the bull and the goat, etc.. He removes from the bull and goat the parts that are offered on the altar, and hands over the rest of their flesh for burning (below 3:7).
and takes out from there the ladle and the fire-pan. The vessels he brought in for the incense.
and puts on ordinary garments and leaves. From the Temple to his home (see below, end of chapter 4).
all these immersions... in the Temple. In the mikveh that was on the roof of one of the chambers in the south of the courtyard (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:17).
in the chol. On the Temple Mount outside the area of the courtyard, beside his chamber (Commentary on the Mishnah, Middot 4:8).

which is only to add to his intention, so that if he remembers an impurity, etc.. This immersion is not an obligation by Torah law but a rule in the Temple that every kohen who begins to serve must immerse beforehand (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 5:4). The reason for this is that he should intend in this immersion to be purified from impurities that he forgot he had contracted (for the law of intention in immersion see also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumah 13:2).
between garments and garments. When he changes from golden garments to white garments and from white garments to golden garments (see also Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 5:7).
elderly or ill. And unable to immerse in cold water.
they heat iron bars. They heat lumps of iron in fire.
from the evening. Before Yom Kippur begins.

for there is no shevut in the Temple. In the Temple, acts that are not a full labor, which the Sages forbade doing on Shabbat, were not prohibited (for this rule see also Hilchot Shabbat 21:27, Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:16). Throwing hot iron lumps into water can cause tempering and hardening of the iron, which is a derivative of the labor of kindling, but since one does not intend to temper, the prohibition is only rabbinic (see Hilchot Shabbat 12:1-2).
they mix hot water into the mikveh water. They heat water on the eve of Yom Kippur and in the morning pour it into the mikveh.
he sanctifies his hands and feet from the laver like the other kohanim. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 5:10.
from a kiton. A flask.
they go up on the east side of the ramp, etc.. The ramp was south of the altar and served for ascending and descending from it, and generally the kohanim went up and down on its sides.
they go up in the middle and down in the middle before the High Priest. The High Priest goes up and down in the middle of the ramp, and other kohanim go up before him to honor him.

the one who won the fire-pan, etc.. The kohen who won the lottery to bring in the fire-pan with the coals for the incense (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 4:5) would gather the coals from the altar in a silver fire-pan and pour them into a golden fire-pan (for details see ibid. 3:5).
its handle. The gripping handle of the fire-pan.
and today it is long. So that his arm will help in carrying it.
three arrangements of fire. Three fires on the altar (for their uses see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 2:4-5).
confession of words. Requesting forgiveness through speech (see Hilchot Teshuvah 1:1; Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:14-15).
you find yourself saying. It is learned from this verse itself, which says: "for himself, and for his household, and for ... Israel."
by himself. For himself.
over his sin-offering bull. Below 3:4.
over the scapegoat. To Azazel (below 3:7, and see also Hilchot Teshuvah 1:2).
and mentions the Name. The explicit Name of the Holy One, blessed be He.
how does he say it. This text is a partial text of the first confession (see below 4:1-2 for the full text of the three confessions).
for sins. Transgressions done unintentionally.
and for iniquities. Transgressions done intentionally.
and for rebellions. Transgressions involving rebellion against God and casting off the yoke, such as desecrating Shabbat and idolatry (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 4:2).
and when he places the lot on the sin-offering goat. See below 3:1.
as it is written, which is the explicit Name. As it is written Yud-Heh-Vav-Heh, and not as it is usually pronounced, "Adonai."
he would raise his voice with the Name. And everyone could hear the explicit Name.

once the unrestrained multiplied. People who were unimportant and not sufficiently upright, who would learn the Name without understanding its matters and use it without consideration (see Hilchot Tefillah 14:10).
and he swallows it in melodies, etc.. He would pronounce the Name in the middle of a tune he sang with his mouth, so that even the kohanim standing nearby did not hear.
kneel, prostrate, and fall on their faces. They go down on their knees and lie on the floor with their hands and feet stretched out and their faces to the ground (see Hilchot Tefillah 5:13).
and they say, blessed is the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever. So they would answer after the mention of the Name in the Temple (see Hilchot Ta'aniyot 4:15-16).

as it is said, "when I call the name of the Lord, give greatness to our God". These are the words of Moses, who told Israel that when he mentions the name of the Lord, they are commanded to give praise to God. From there the obligation to do so always is learned.
and in the three confessions he would intend, etc.. When he finished saying the confession with the verse "before the Lord you shall be purified."

,. He intended to say the name of God together with those standing in the courtyard who responded "blessed is the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever," and then he finished and said to them "you shall be purified," as a sign that God atoned for them and purified them.
and for the confession of the burned bulls. The confession said over the bull of the anointed kohen and the bull for the unwitting communal error.
the two lots. Mentioned in the Torah, to be placed on the two goats to determine which of them will be offered to God and which sent to Azazel (Leviticus 16:8).

and he should not intend. If the lot for God came up in the right hand, it would be a good sign, and so that the High Priest would not feel the lots and deliberately bring up the lot for God in his right hand, he had to put both his hands together into the lots' vessel (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 39a and Rashi there).
and this vessel is ordinary and was of wood. It is not considered one of the service vessels of the Temple (and therefore it is permitted to make it of wood - see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 1:18).
and the High Priest comes there. After he confessed over the bull between the Ulam and the altar (below 4:1).
and the segan. The kohen who is the deputy of the High Priest (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:16).
and the head of the father's house. The kohen at the head of the watch serving that day in the Temple (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:11).
shook. Mixed the lots.
and the lottery is indispensable. If he consecrated the goats not by lottery, the goats were not consecrated.

and the lottery is indispensable even though it is not a service. Although it is not considered part of the system of services in the Temple (such as bringing offerings, incense, and lighting the menorah), it is essential and without it the service of the goats cannot be done.
and drawing the lots from the basket is invalid by a stranger. A Yisrael who is not a kohen.

a strand of crimson wool. A piece of wool dyed with the red color extracted from the tola'at shani worm. After the goat was sent off, sometimes its color changed to white as a sign that Israel's sins were atoned for, as it says: "if your sins are like scarlet (the color shani), they shall be made white as snow" (Isaiah 1:18, Mishnah Shabbat 9:3).
the weight of two sela. The weight of two coins called sela (about 34 grams).
and stands it opposite the place of its sending. Facing the eastern gate of the courtyard, through which it was taken out to Azazel.

and the slaughtered one opposite its place of slaughter. He stands the goat to be slaughtered facing the place where it will be slaughtered, close to the north of the altar (R. Y. Kafih, Orah VeSimchah).
and sprinkles from the blood of both of them on this day forty-three sprinklings. See also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:11-12; for the details of the order of sprinklings see below 4:2.
the poles of the Ark. The carrying poles on both sides of the Ark of the Covenant.

close to the kapporet by a tefach. The kapporet is the golden cover placed on the Ark. The thickness of the kapporet is a tefach, and the sprinkling of the blood must be opposite its thickness and not on its top.
one upward and seven downward. He flicks the blood with his finger upward once, and downward seven times.

for this which is said "seven times" is in addition to the first sprinkling. The verse says "and he shall sprinkle with his finger on the face of the kapporet eastward," and afterward it says "and before the kapporet he shall sprinkle seven times" (Leviticus 16:14). By tradition we learn that this means seven sprinklings in addition to the first sprinkling mentioned at the beginning of the verse.

one, one and one, etc.. For the upper sprinkling he would say "one." Then for the first lower sprinkling he would say "one and one," up to the seventh sprinkling, for which he would say "one and seven."

for so it is said regarding the blood of the bull, on the kapporet and before the kapporet. This verse is said regarding the goat and also deals with throwing the blood between the poles, and the commentators struggled with how the law of sprinkling on the curtain is learned from here, and explained in various ways.
and counts the way he counted inside. "One," "one and one," "one and two," etc.

he does not intend with them to sprinkle either upward or downward but like one who whips. Some explained that he would not sprinkle the sprinklings at a specific place (up or down), just as one who strikes his fellow does not intend to hit him in a specific spot (Meiri, Yoma 15a). Others explained that he changes his hand's position from sprinkling upward to sprinkling downward, just as one who strikes his fellow changes the position of his hand to hit him from the front and the back (Sefer HaYashar no. 307).
and afterward he mixes, etc.. Below 4:2.
from both of them. Together when they are mixed.
on the four horns of the golden altar in the Sanctuary. On the corners of the inner altar on which incense is burned every day.
on the middle of this altar. On the middle of the top of the altar.
dips his finger in the blood, a dip for each sprinkling. See Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:8.

and the remainder of the blood he pours on the western base of the outer altar. The blood that remained he would pour on the lower part of the altar outside the Sanctuary (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:11).
and all are fit. Also Israelites and not only kohanim.
a fixed practice. A permanent arrangement.
and up to the beginning of the wilderness. Close to the place of sending the goat, as explained next.

and one man rests, etc.. On Shabbat and Yom Kippur a person is forbidden to leave the city or the place where he is resting beyond a distance of a mil (two thousand cubits - see Hilchot Shabbat 27:1). Since the place where the goat was taken was far from Jerusalem, they made booths such that the distance between them did not exceed a mil, so that people resting in a booth could accompany it to the next booth.

they stand at the end of the boundary. The end of the area where they are permitted to walk, for the place of sending the goat was two mil from the last booth, and the people of the booth were allowed to walk only a mil (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 6:4).
divides. Splits in two.

half of it he ties to the rock. The reason is that if he cannot see whether the crimson strand tied to the goat turned white, he will see it on the strand tied to the rock (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 6:6, based on the Gemara).
and the dedaviyot. Lookout posts.
and they wave with cloths. From one lookout to the next.
so that they will know. Those standing in the Temple.
a goat to the wilderness. To the cliff.
returns. The High Priest.
their sacrificial parts. The parts that were offered on the altar.
and puts them in a vessel and burns them on the altar. He would put the sacrificial parts in a vessel in order to burn them afterward on the altar (see below 4:2).
large pieces joined to one another in the manner of a braid. He would not cut the limbs all the way through but leave them somewhat connected to one another.
and they cut them up there in their hides. They cut the limbs without flaying the hide.
as we explained. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:2.
as we explained. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:5.
is not a service; therefore if he wished, etc.. For no service is performed except in priestly garments (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 10:4).
and if he wished to read in white garments. In the special service garments of Yom Kippur, for he was wearing them for the services of the bull and the goats.
as we explained. Ibid. 8:11.

and the synagogue attendant takes a Torah scroll and gives it to the head of the synagogue, and the head of the synagogue gives it to the segan, etc.. They would pass the scroll from person to person to show the importance of the High Priest (similarly see Hilchot Chagigah 3:4). The synagogue attendant is the sexton of the synagogue, and the head of the synagogue is the synagogue's administrator (see Orah VeSimchah about which synagogue is meant). The segan is the deputy of the kohanim, the second to the High Priest.
Acharei Mot. The order of the Yom Kippur service mentioned there (Leviticus chapter 16).
and "but on the tenth" in the portion of the festivals. The passage that details the laws of Yom Kippur in the portion Emor (Leviticus 23:26-32).
and rolls up the Torah. Closes the Torah scroll.
and says more than I read, etc.. So as not to cast an aspersion on the Torah scroll: when people see him continuing to read by heart, they will not say that the scroll is lacking.
and "on the tenth" in the Book of Numbers, etc.. Numbers 29:7-11.

because one does not roll a Torah scroll in public, and why not, etc.. They did not roll the Torah scroll from the Book of Leviticus, in the portion Emor, to the Book of Numbers, because one should not roll a Torah scroll from place to place because of the burden on the public, and to bring another scroll open to Numbers is impossible because when one person reads from two scrolls, people might think that he switched scrolls because the first was invalid (see Hilchot Tefillah 12:23). Between the portion Acharei Mot and the portion "but on the tenth," however, they did roll the scroll, since they are adjacent and deal with one subject (see Hilchot Tefillah 12:8).
blesses before it and after it as they bless in the synagogue. Before it "who chose us," after it "who gave us the Torah of truth" (Hilchot Tefillah 12:5).
and adds after it seven blessings. Similar to the blessings the king recites after reading the Torah at the Hakhel ceremony (Hilchot Chagigah 3:4).
three blessings as instituted. As we pray every day in the Amidah.
on the Temple, a blessing by itself. A special blessing not combined with other subjects.
and a request according to what he is accustomed. In this request he pleads and prays before God as he is able.
finds the curtain slightly open. A little open.
between the two poles. The carrying poles on both sides of the Ark of the Covenant.

and in the Second Temple, where there was no Ark, he would place it on the Foundation Stone. A stone on the western side of the Holy of Holies on which the Ark used to rest (Beit HaBechirah 4:1). It is called "shetiyah" from the word for foundation, "for the place of the service is the foundation of the world" (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 5:1 there; and the Gemara in Yoma 54b explained "that from it the world was founded").

and he holds the rim of the ladle, etc.. He had to place the incense from the palms of his hands onto the coals. To transfer the incense from the ladle to his palms he had to hold the edge of the ladle with his fingertips or his teeth, and with his thumbs he transferred the incense into his palms until all of the incense returned and filled his palms as it was when he scooped it.

on the inner side of the fire-pan so that, etc.. He would place the incense on the inner side of the fire-pan, the side far from him, so that he not be burned by the smoke rising from the incense after placing it on the coals (see also Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:8).
and waits there until the House fills with smoke. As it says: "and he shall put the incense on the fire before the Lord, and the cloud of incense shall cover..." (Leviticus 16:13).
and he walks backward... his face to the Holy and his back to the Sanctuary. This is out of reverence (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:4).
lest they say he died in the Sanctuary. For many High Priests died in the Sanctuary because they were unworthy or changed the incense service (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 5:1).
that if this year is parched, let it be rainy. If it was decreed that the year would be hot, that it also be rainy.
a scepter from the house of Judah. Rule from the tribe of Judah.
need sustenance. So that they not need the help of others.
the prayer of travelers. Who pray that rain not fall on them.

they cast lots for the removal of the ashes. Every day they held lotteries ("payisot") among the kohanim to divide the day's services among them (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 4:1). On Yom Kippur they held only the first lottery, which determined who would remove part of the ashes from the altar (terumat hadeshen - ibid. 4:5).

and arrange the pile and clear the ashes from the altar. After the removal of the ashes, the other kohanim would clean the altar of the remaining ashes on it, and the kohen who cleared the altar would arrange the fires of the altar.
in the order we explained. Ibid. 2:10-13, 6:1.
linen. Flax.
for the service of the day is in linen garments. For the special services of Yom Kippur are done in white garments made of linen.

and he slaughters the tamid, the majority of two, etc.. In slaughtering an animal one ideally cuts both signs of slaughter (the windpipe and the gullet), but if he cut the majority of the windpipe and gullet the slaughter is valid (Hilchot Shechitah 1:9-10). On Yom Kippur the High Priest must himself receive the blood of the slaughter, and therefore he slaughters only the majority of the two signs and gives another to finish, so that he can receive the blood immediately.
as in the whole order of the daily tamid that we explained. Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 6:3-7.
he offers the bull and the seven lambs of the musaf of the day. Above 1:1, Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 10:1.
and comes to his bull. The sin-offering bull that comes from the High Priest's own funds.
between the Ulam and the altar. East of the Ulam and west of the altar, at the north of the altar.
its head to the south and its face to the west. Its head and body toward the south, and its face turned toward the west.
and the kohen stands in the east and his face to the west. East of the bull, with his face toward the west.
and leans... and confesses. Like the leaning and confession of an individual who brings an offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:14-15).
and so he would say. For the details of the recitation of the confessions see above 2:6-7.
and afterward he casts lots, etc.. As explained above 3:1-4.
and gives it to the one who stirs it so that it does not congeal. The High Priest would give the blood to someone who would stir it so that it would not congeal while he performed other services.

on the fourth row of the Sanctuary from outside. The one who stirred the blood would stand on the fourth row of paving stones outside the Sanctuary (Rashi). Some explain that this means the fourth uppermost group of paving stones on the steps of the Ulam close to the Sanctuary (Responsa of Rama MiPano no. 11; and see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 4:9 in Piskei VeShitot).

as it is said, "from upon the altar before the Lord". "And he shall take a fire-pan full of coals of fire from upon the altar before the Lord." From this we learn that one must take the coals from the western side of the altar, which is closer to the Sanctuary.
incense fine as can be. The incense burned every day was ground to be fine, and the Yom Kippur incense was ground again so that it would be extremely fine (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 2:3).

not leveled and not heaped but tightly packed. He gathers some of the incense in his two palms and fills them neither sparingly nor excessively but in exact measure (some explain that "tefufot" means with slightly extra - Rashi, Meiri).

the large according to his size and the small according to his size. The measure of the scoop was according to the size of the High Priest's palms, and there was no uniform measure for the incense burned.
we already explained. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 5:18.

therefore by law he should carry, etc.. Since he must carry with both hands, it would have been proper that carrying the ladle, which holds the incense and is the essence of the commandment, be done with the right hand, while carrying the fire-pan, which is only to burn the incense on it, be done with the left.
and moreover it is hot. And he cannot hold the handle near the fire-pan itself in a way that would make it easier to carry.
to bear it. To carry it.
and at the time of giving the blood in the Sanctuary. At the time of giving the blood of the inner sin offerings.
as we explained in Hilchot Temidin. Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:3.
and sprinkles from it there. For the details of the order of the sprinklings see above 3:5-6.

on a golden stand that was there. A stand made of gold (the basin in which they received the blood of the offerings was pointed at the bottom so it could not be put down on the floor - see Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:13).
and slaughters the goat. The sin-offering goat for which the lot came up to be offered to God.

and stands inside the golden altar between the altar and the menorah. The commentators struggled to explain this halakhah. Some emended it to "and stands before the golden altar" (Radbaz, Mayim Chayim; and compare Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:14). According to this, the High Priest stood east of the golden altar at its southeast corner, opposite the gap between the altar and the menorah (for the golden altar stood in the middle of the Sanctuary, and the menorah was drawn toward the south wall, west of the altar). Others explained that he stood west of the altar (see Riva, Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:14).

and he goes around and sprinkles on the horns from outside. The kohen would stand in his place and circle the altar with his hand and sprinkle on the outer side of the horns (Mayim Chayim, and see Riva; some explain that he would circle the altar with his feet - see Kesef Mishneh and Likutei Halakhot, Yoma 59a).

and on all of them he gives from below upward, etc.. On the three horns that were not in front of him he would sprinkle by raising his hand from below upward, but on the southeast horn, which was in front of him, he sprinkled from above downward, for had he sprinkled from below upward there was a concern that the blood would fall on his garments.
on the purity of the altar. On the altar itself and not on the ashes and coals on it (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:12).
in the place where the gifts of its horns were completed. The place where he finished sprinkling on the horns, in the south.
and leans both his hands on its head. See Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:10.
sends the goat to the wilderness, etc.. See above 3:7-8.
the goat done outside... his ram and the people's ram. See above 1:1.
and burns the sacrificial parts of the bull and goat that are burned. See above 3:7.
and takes out the ladle and the fire-pan. Of the incense that he burned on his first entry.
and burns the incense of between the evenings... like the other days. Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 6:11.
in the order we explained. Above chapter 4.
he has done nothing. He has not fulfilled his obligation.
the requirement of the inside is like the service of the inside. Scooping the incense is for the purpose of burning it inside.

the ram and the goat of the musafim, etc.. His ram, the people's ram, and the sin-offering goat, which are offered after the services performed inside. Although their offering is an outside service, if he put them before the inside service, the inside service is displaced by them, and therefore he did not fulfill his obligation.
he should bring another goat and slaughter it. For the slaughter of the goat must come after the throwing of the bull's blood in the Holy of Holies.
in the gifts. In the sprinklings of the blood.
he should bring other blood. He should slaughter another animal, bring its blood, and begin sprinkling from the beginning.
and began with the gifts in the Sanctuary. The sprinklings on the curtain.

for all of them are each a separate atonement. Each of the series of sprinklings (Holy of Holies, curtain, altar) is a separate atonement. Therefore there is no need to begin from the beginning of all the sprinklings but only from the beginning of the series in which he is.
for pouring the remainder... is not indispensable. Even if he did not pour out the remaining blood at all, he has fulfilled his obligation (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 19:4).

If the blood of the bull etc.. Since the incense is to be burned after the bull is slaughtered, if the bull's blood was spilled and another bull must be slaughtered and the sprinklings begun again (as explained above in halachot 5-7), one must also take a further handful of incense in order to burn it again after the bull's slaughter.

And he takes a handful of the incense a second time before the slaughter of the bull. From the Rambam here it appears that the handful is taken before the bull is slaughtered. However, it was already explained (above, halacha 2) that they would first slaughter the bull and afterwards take the handful. The Kesef Mishneh and others emended the text and wrote that the reading should be "after the slaughter of the bull." Other commentators left the text as it is but explained that it means he takes the handful only after the bull's slaughter (see Orah VeSimchah). Rabbi Yehoshua HaNagid wrote that in this case (where he already slaughtered the first bull and took the handful after it) the handful may be taken even before the slaughter (Responsa of Rabbi Yehoshua HaNagid, no. 66, cited in the Kesef Mishneh; and see Chesed LeAvraham, who explained similarly).

He does not render garments impure, and it is not burned at the Beit HaDeshen etc.. The bull and the goat were burned outside Jerusalem at the Beit HaDeshen (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:4), and whoever touches them or carries them from the time they leave the wall of the Temple courtyard becomes impure and renders impure the garments he touches them with (Hilchot Parah 5:4-5). Since the blood of the first bull was spilled, these laws do not apply to it, and it is burned within the courtyard like other disqualified sanctified animals (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:3).
Before he finishes the sprinklings etc.. Before he finishes the sprinklings that he sprinkles from the blood of the bull and the blood of the goat separately (above 4:2).

He gives one above and seven below for the bull etc.. He continues to sprinkle from the mixed blood the applications of the bull and the applications of the goat until he completes one above and seven below for the bull, and after them one above and seven below for the goat. Every sprinkling he sprinkles contains both blood of the bull and blood of the goat, and therefore when he intends it for the bull the sprinklings count for the bull, and when he intends it for the goat the sprinklings count for the goat.

They became mixed at the last application etc.. Before he sprinkled the last sprinkling from the blood of the bull. In this case (and likewise in the other cases where the blood became mixed after the bull's sprinklings had begun) there is no need to start again from the beginning of the sequence; it is enough that he sprinkle the last application from the mixture for the bull.

And some of the cups became mixed and the cup of the bull's blood is not known etc.. One cup of the bull and one cup of the goat are known, and the two other cups are not known to be of the bull or of the goat.

And those cups that became mixed are to be poured into the channel. They are to be poured into the water channel in the Temple, like other blood found in the courtyard that drains there (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:11-12).
The Omnipresent has relinquished His ownership etc.. The Holy One, blessed be He, made all the kohanim partners as owners in this bull (see also Hilchot Temurah 1:10).

A sin offering whose owners died is to die etc.. A sin offering animal whose owners died is not offered, and its law is that it must die (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1). But since all the kohanim are partners in the Yom Kippur bull, even if the High Priest dies the sin offering is not considered a sin offering whose owners died.
In appearance, in height and in price. In general appearance, in size and in monetary value.
And their purchase as one. He should buy both of them together.

And he shall cast lots over them as at the beginning. He casts lots to choose which of them will be the partner of the goat that did not die, since a goat cannot be taken without a lottery (see above 3:3).

And the second... shall graze until it develops a blemish etc.. Since it was consecrated as an offering, it must be redeemed. They wait until it develops a blemish so that it can be redeemed by sale, and the sale proceeds are given to the collection boxes from which voluntary burnt offerings are bought.

For a communal sin offering does not die. If the goat were an individual's sin offering, its law would be to die, like a sin offering whose owners achieved atonement through another; but this law does not apply to a communal sin offering (for the laws of the sin offering that dies see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin chapter 4).
The bull and the goat of Yom Kippur that were lost. See also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:2.
That they become defiled. That a blemish occurs in them.
A blemish disqualifies the scapegoat. Even though it is not offered on the altar, a blemish disqualifies it like an offering.
Even a temporary blemish. A blemish that will heal in the future; even such a blemish disqualifies the offering (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:5).
Lacking in time. A disqualification that is not in the animal's body but relates to the time of its offering (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 18:8).

For example, one whose mother was slaughtered for a sick person on Yom Kippur etc.. An animal whose mother was slaughtered on the same day is forbidden to be slaughtered and is disqualified as an offering until the next day (Hilchot Shechitah 12:1). Although generally the prohibition applies only to slaughter and not to killing in other ways (ibid. 12:3), pushing the goat to Azazel is considered like slaughter, and is forbidden.
A treifah. An animal that is about to die because of a defect or a wound and the like.
He mounts it on his shoulder. Even though it is forbidden to carry on Yom Kippur (Hilchot Shevitat Asor 1:2).
He enters the Temple and takes it. Even though it is forbidden for an impure person to enter the Temple.
And he shall kill it in any way that kills it. He may kill it in any manner he wishes.
It was diminished. It was lessened.
As it says, "in the Tent of Meeting". And a tent without a roof is not a tent (this verse was said regarding the inner sprinklings of the bull of the anointed kohen).
An altar that was not inaugurated with incense. On which incense was never burned (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:1).

One of its ingredients. The incense was composed of eleven ingredients (Hilchot Kli HaMikdash 2:2); if one of them is missing, the incense is deficient and whoever burns it is liable to death at the hands of Heaven (ibid. 2:8).

Or the smoke-raiser. In addition to the ingredients of the incense, they would add to it a herb that caused its smoke to rise like a staff. If it was not added to the incense, one who burns it is liable to death, since this causes the High Priest to appear before God in the Holy of Holies without the incense cloud rising.

He is liable to death for his entry without a mitzvah. For this is the law of the High Priest: if he enters the Holy of Holies not for the sake of a mitzvah, he is liable to death at the hands of Heaven (see Hilchot Biat HaMikdash 2:3).

Therefore, if he entered inadvertently and burned deliberately, or etc.. Although he has no liability for entering without need, since he was inadvertent, or he also brought in complete incense, he is liable for the deficient incense if he burned it.
Taking a handful of the incense is a service, and intention disqualifies it etc.. Just as intention disqualifies in the service of an offering (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 13:1).
For the preparations of an offering are like the offering. Even though the placing of the coals is not a service, intention disqualifies it, since it is a preparatory act for the burning.

He took a handful with the tips of his fingers. In taking the handful of incense, the kohen would bury his palms in the incense, bring his hands together and gather up the incense. If he did not bury his hands in the incense but rested his palms on the incense and gathered it with his fingers.
From the sides. He put the incense into his palms from the sides using his thumbs.
From below upward. He placed the back of his hand on the incense and raised the incense into his hands with his fingers.
Or he took a handful with this hand and with that hand and brought them together. He took a handful with his two hands separately and then joined them together.
